title: multibagger_case_studies › Multibagger Case Studies & the "Second-Order Thinking" Process

body:
- **The same pattern, different outcomes:** Suzlon (2005–08) and Inox Wind/renewables, the infra/power capex boom of 2007–08 (Lanco, GVK, JP Associates **[UNVERIFIED specific outcomes]**), and Yes Bank / DHFL as "Bajaj Finance look-alikes" in lending **[UNVERIFIED]** all had a policy or sector tailwind, fast growth and a high multiple. What separated them from Eicher, Radico and Bajaj Finance was mostly **leverage, governance and the capital-allocation discipline of the promoter**. That fits Mayer's "avoid debt so drawdowns aren't permanent" rule.
- **Practical base rate:** with about 2–4% of stocks creating all net wealth, a "multibagger playbook" should be judged on portfolio outcomes (a few big winners paying for many losers) and on position-sizing rules that survive 50–90% drawdowns, not on hit rate.
- **Hindsight trap:** each case study selects on the outcome. For each signal (policy shift, competitor distress, capex announcement), the counterfactual cases where it fired and the stock failed should be logged too, for example the solar/wind PLI and the China+1 chemical names that derated in 2022–25.

`case_study:symphony-2009-2018` · tickers: SYMPHONY · confidence: verified

Split/bonus-adjusted ₹3.9 (Jan 2009) → ATH ₹2,099 (Jan 2018) ≈540x. In the measurable 2012–18 leg (19x), standalone P/E rose 15 → 84 (5.5x) × implied EPS ~3.5x, so about 58% was rerating. Early signal (narrative partly unverified): after a mid-2000s turnaround it became the asset-light, outsourced leader in branded air coolers, with OPM 25–31% and ROCE ~50% (screener FY15–18). The stock went 10x in 2009–10 alone. Ended: EPS was flat at ~₹17–23 for FY17–FY23 while P/E stayed 50–75 (weather-dependent single category, more competition, overseas acquisitions in Mexico and Australia). FY26: consolidated net loss ~₹141 cr after a ₹173 cr goodwill impairment on the Australian business (Climate Holdings) plus ₹35 cr PPE/intangible impairments; standalone loss ₹166 cr after a ₹298 cr investment write-down. The stock fell −77% to ₹491 (Oct 2026); ₹554 on 19 Nov 2026. Lesson: a seasonal single-product franchise at 80x with flat EPS, plus foreign acquisitions, gives a long bear market. Watch for EPS stagnation at a premium P/E, and capital allocation outside the core.

Key data: **start_year**: 2009; **end_year**: 2018; **start_price**: 3.9; **end_price**: 2099; **price_nov2026**: 554; **multiple**: ~540x (19x in 2012-18); **pe_start**: 15.3; **pe_end**: 83.6; **eps_multiple_implied**: ~3.5x (2012-18); **max_drawdown**: -42% in run; -77% after; **early_signals**: asset-light category leader, ROCE ~50%; **ended**: flat EPS at 50-80x; Australia impairments FY26; **lesson**: diworsification + flat EPS at premium P/E

title: UNIPARTS › 6. Full ledger

body:
`person:group-jaypee` · flag: **severe** · confidence: verified · tickers: JPASSOCIAT, JPPOWER, JPINFRATEC

Flag: SEVERE. Cement-hydro-real-estate-expressway group that borrowed heavily in 2007-2012. Jaypee Infratech (JIL, Yamuna Expressway + ~20,000+ unfinished Noida flats) was among RBI's first 12 IBC referrals (2017, IDBI-led); its listed equity was extinguished; NCLT approved Suraksha group's plan (Mar-2023). Key finding: the Supreme Court (Feb-2020, Anuj Jain v Axis Bank) upheld that JIL's mortgage of ~858 acres to secure the parent Jaiprakash Associates' (JAL) loans were preferential transactions to be avoided -- a listed subsidiary's assets pledged for the parent's debt. Homebuyer funds: ED arrested MD Manoj Gaur (13-Nov-2025) alleging ~Rs 12,000 cr of homebuyer money was diverted/siphoned, partly to Jaypee Sewa Sansthan (a trust he heads); he reportedly surrendered in Feb-2026 after bail rejection (single-source). Charges are allegations pending trial. JAL itself went into IBC; CoC approved Adani Enterprises' ~Rs 14,535 cr plan with 93.8% votes (Nov-2025), NCLT approved (17-Mar-2026), NCLAT dismissed Vedanta's challenge (4-May-2026) -- JAL equity holders expected to get little or nothing. Jaiprakash Power Ventures went through lender-led debt-for-equity conversion and remains listed. Early signals (visible by 2012-14): customer advances funding other businesses, inter-group guarantees and mortgages, repeated asset sales to service debt, rising promoter pledges. Lesson: in real-estate groups, homebuyer advances are the first pot of money diverted.

- **regulator findings:** SC 2020: JIL mortgages for JAL = preferential transactions
- **allegations:** ED 2025: Rs 12,000 cr homebuyer-fund diversion (pending trial)

| Days (HSIE basis, on sales) | FY22 | FY23 | FY24 | FY25 | FY26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory | 79 | 72 | 60 | 63 | 57 |
| Payables | 95 | 72 | 50 | 50 | 46 |
| Cash conversion cycle | −9 | 6 | 19 | 13 | 11 |
(Screener on COGS basis, FY26: inventory 80, payables 64.)

- Payables fell faster than inventory (95→46 days). Possible reasons: deliberately paying contract manufacturers faster for better prices (a positive), MSME 45-day payment rules (Sec 43B(h) from FY24), or post-buyout normalisation. **Open question** for management and the vendor scuttlebutt (§5).
- All manufacturing is outsourced to third-party contract manufacturers `[BRSR26]`. Vendors absorb about 50% of raw-material inflation `[HSIE]`. That shows purchasing power, and it is also a pressure point on vendors: ask them.
- Supply chain `[HSIE]`: one central DC (6–7 days of inventory) plus 17 third-party regional warehouses of 60–65 stores each, capacity about 1,000–1,100 stores. VMM is moving to 4 hubs; a 600k sq ft Haryana DC is live. RFID tags cost ₹15 each, on items above ₹200, reused 10–15 times.
